title: The first night after pulmonary thromboendarterectomy
subtitle: A 48-year-old woman on postoperative day 0 after bilateral pulmonary thromboendarterectomy under deep hypothermic circulatory arrest, with a PA catheter in place and oxygenation that has started to slip.
objectives: Take a structured handoff after pulmonary thromboendarterectomy and state which intraoperative facts (circulatory arrest periods, hemodynamics off bypass, the PVR change, the surgeon's view of the specimen) predict the first night.
Set up ventilation, fluid, hemodynamic, and neurological management for the first 24 hours after PTE and justify why routine pulmonary vasodilators are not part of it.
Recognize reperfusion lung injury, distinguish it from fluid overload, pneumonia, and airway bleeding, and state what is and is not supported in its management.

Separate residual pulmonary hypertension with RV dysfunction from reperfusion injury, select vasoactive support that protects RV coronary perfusion, and name the point at which VA ECMO becomes the right answer.

Manage airway hemorrhage after PTE, including bronchoscopic localization, lung isolation, the anticoagulation question, and ECMO as a rescue, and explain what each of these events means for the patient's long-term outcome.

stages.title: Presentation
stages.narrative:
A 48-year-old woman with chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension diagnosed after two years of unexplained exertional dyspnea underwent bilateral pulmonary thromboendarterectomy today. Preoperative right heart catheterization showed a markedly elevated mean PA pressure and PVR with a preserved cardiac index on no pulmonary vasodilator therapy. CT and conventional angiography showed proximal disease on the right and more segmental disease on the left. [REVIEW]

The operation was done on cardiopulmonary bypass with cooling to deep hypothermia and two periods of circulatory arrest, one per side, each within the usual limit with a reperfusion interval between them. The surgeon describes a good right-sided specimen with a clear distal tail and a less satisfying left side with more distal, segmental material. Coming off bypass the PA pressure had fallen substantially and the PVR had roughly halved on a low-dose inotrope and a small dose of vasopressor. TEE at the end of the case showed a dilated but contracting RV, no significant tricuspid regurgitation, and a septum that was less flattened than at the start. [REVIEW]

She arrives in the CTICU intubated, with a PA catheter, a radial arterial line, two chest tubes, and epicardial pacing wires. She is still rewarming. Ninety minutes after arrival, the FiO2 has been increased twice to maintain saturations and the peak airway pressure has drifted up. The resident asks whether to start inhaled nitric oxide. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: List the facts you need from the surgical and anesthesia handoff that will predict tonight, and then set up the patient: PA catheter use, ventilation, fluids, hemodynamic targets, and what you will do about the resident's question. Commit before revealing.
questions.modelAnswer:
**The handoff.** Most of what will happen tonight was decided in the operating room, so the handoff is a prediction exercise.

- **How many circulatory arrest periods and how long,** and the lowest temperature reached. Total arrest time and the number of periods are the exposure for neurological injury and, in some series, for the degree of reperfusion lung injury. [REVIEW]
- **The specimen.** The UCSD classification of the surgical findings (from proximal, well-organized material with a clear distal tail to distal, segmental, or subsegmental disease and microvascular disease) is the best intraoperative predictor of whether the PVR will fall and whether residual pulmonary hypertension will be the problem tonight. A surgeon who is unhappy with one side is telling you where the residual PH will come from. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]
- **The PVR change.** Preoperative versus post-bypass PA pressure, PVR, and cardiac output. A PVR that fell substantially is the expected good outcome. A PVR that did not fall despite a good specimen predicts residual PH and a difficult night. The post-bypass numbers are also the baseline against which every later PA catheter reading is judged. [REVIEW]
- **Hemodynamics coming off bypass.** Inotrope and vasopressor requirement, whether the RV needed help, whether there was any difficulty separating, and whether any pulmonary vasodilator was used in the OR.
- **Airway bleeding on the table.** Any blood in the endotracheal tube on reperfusion, any need for a bronchial blocker, and what the surgeon thinks of the distal endarterectomy planes. This is the single fact that most changes the anticoagulation and ECMO calculus later.
- **Bypass and clamp times, transfusion, coagulopathy, and the protamine response.**
- **Neurological:** pupils at the end of the case, whether the patient moved on emergence from hypothermia, and the EEG or cerebral oximetry story during arrest if the center uses them.

**Setting up the patient.**

- **PA catheter.** It stays, and it is used. The questions it answers tonight are: is the PVR rising (residual PH or reperfusion injury raising pulmonary vascular tone), is the cardiac output falling (RV failure), and is the wedge pressure low (which it should be, and which helps distinguish reperfusion edema from hydrostatic edema). Trend, not single numbers. [REVIEW]
- **Ventilation.** Lung-protective tidal volumes, moderate PEEP, and a target that avoids both hypoxemia and hypercapnia because each raises PVR and each is a direct insult to the RV. This is one of the few patients in whom permissive hypercapnia is not an acceptable tradeoff. Avoid excessive PEEP and high plateau pressures, which raise RV afterload through a different mechanism. Plan for a period of ventilation rather than early extubation, because reperfusion injury peaks over the first 24 to 72 hours and an early extubation that fails costs more than a planned delay. The UCSD program's practice has been to keep patients ventilated at least overnight and to extubate when oxygenation is stable and improving. [VERIFY] [NMH protocol, insert]
- **Fluids.** Restrictive. The endarterectomized segments have fresh, denuded vascular surfaces and increased permeability, so every milliliter of excess intravascular volume is a milliliter that can leak into reperfused lung. Diuresis is started early once the patient is warm and hemodynamically stable. The RV, however, is preload-dependent and the balance is set by the PA catheter: cardiac output and wedge, not CVP. Colloid versus crystalloid and transfusion thresholds are institutional. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW]
- **Hemodynamics.** The targets are a systemic pressure that preserves RV coronary perfusion, a cardiac index that reflects an RV keeping up, and a PVR that is not rising. Vasopressor to protect systemic pressure, inotrope only if the cardiac output is inadequate. Sinus rhythm or AV pacing. [REVIEW]
- **Neurological.** Hourly neurological checks as soon as sedation allows, with an early wake-up test to look for focal deficit. Temperature management to avoid rebound hyperthermia during rewarming, which worsens any ischemic injury incurred during arrest. Glucose control. Delirium and short-term cognitive change are common after DHCA and usually resolve, but a focal deficit or a failure to wake is a reason for imaging, not for waiting. [REVIEW]
- **Anticoagulation.** Heparin is resumed early (typically the first postoperative night when bleeding has settled) because the patient has a lifelong thrombotic disorder and fresh endarterectomy surfaces. The timing is a conversation with the surgeon and is institutional. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW]

**The resident's question.** Not yet, and the reason is worth saying out loud. Inhaled nitric oxide is a pulmonary vasodilator. The patient's problem is early hypoxemia with rising airway pressures in the first hours after reperfusion, which is far more likely to be the beginning of reperfusion lung injury than a pulmonary vasoconstrictor problem. iNO would improve V/Q matching in the perfused lung and might help oxygenation, and it is used widely in these patients, but it does not treat the injury, it adds a device and a weaning problem, and a trial of iNO before the diagnosis is clear can muddy the hemodynamic picture. If the PA pressure and PVR are rising and the RV is struggling, iNO is a reasonable move. If the problem is oxygenation alone, the first steps are ventilator optimization and diuresis. The UCSD program's published approach does not use routine pulmonary vasodilators after PTE and reserves them for residual PH with hemodynamic compromise. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]

stages.title: New data
stages.narrative:
Six hours after arrival. The FiO2 is now high and the PEEP has been increased. The chest radiograph shows new patchy airspace opacities in the right lower and middle lobes and the left lower lobe, corresponding to the segments the surgeon described as best endarterectomized on the right and to the left lower lobe. The upper lobes are relatively spared. [REVIEW]

PA catheter: PA pressures are modestly higher than the post-bypass values but well below the preoperative numbers. Wedge pressure is low. Cardiac index is adequate on the same low-dose inotrope. Systemic pressure is maintained on a low-dose vasopressor. [REVIEW]

The endotracheal tube has small amounts of pink, frothy secretions on suctioning. There is no frank blood. Chest tube output is modest. Temperature is normal. White count is unremarkable for a postoperative patient. Net fluid balance since the OR is positive by about a liter and a half, most of it in the operating room. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: What is this, what else could it be, and what do you do about it? Be explicit about which of the common interventions (diuresis, steroids, iNO, prone positioning, ECMO) are supported, which are habit, and the order you would use them.
questions.modelAnswer:
**This is reperfusion pulmonary edema, now usually called reperfusion lung injury.** The pattern is the diagnosis: new airspace opacities confined to the segments that were endarterectomized, appearing within the first 24 hours, with a low wedge pressure, no fever, and pink frothy secretions. The endarterectomized segments have been reperfused at full pressure through a denuded vascular bed after months or years of hypoperfusion, and the result is a high-permeability edema that is histologically a localized ARDS. In the UCSD experience it occurs in a substantial minority of patients, with the reported incidence varying with the definition used, and it is the leading cause of early morbidity after PTE. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]

**The differential and how to separate it:**

- **Hydrostatic edema from volume.** The patient is a liter and a half positive. Against it: the wedge is low, and the distribution is segmental rather than diffuse and dependent. For it: a liter and a half is a lot in a patient with leaky lungs, and the two coexist. The practical answer is that diuresis is indicated either way. [REVIEW]
- **Pneumonia or aspiration.** Six hours is early for a ventilator-associated process. No fever, no purulence. Culture the secretions and do not start antibiotics for a radiograph. [REVIEW]
- **Airway bleeding.** Pink froth is edema fluid. Frank blood or clot is a different problem with a different stage of this case. Bronchoscopy answers the question if there is any doubt. [REVIEW]
- **Residual pulmonary hypertension with RV failure.** The PA pressure is up only modestly and the cardiac index is fine. This is not the picture, but the distinction matters and is the subject of the next stage.
- **Reperfusion injury in a steal pattern.** A subtlety: after PTE, blood is redistributed from the previously perfused segments to the newly opened ones, which can produce V/Q mismatch and hypoxemia without edema. Pulmonary artery steal is a recognized finding and usually resolves over weeks. It does not produce infiltrates. [VERIFY]

**Management, in order of what is supported:**

1. **Ventilation.** Lung-protective ventilation with enough PEEP to recruit the injured segments and an FiO2 that keeps the patient out of hypoxemia. The constraint, unlike in ordinary ARDS, is that hypercapnia raises PVR and PEEP raises RV afterload, so the usual tradeoffs are tighter. Ventilate as for ARDS but with the RV in the room. [REVIEW]
2. **Diuresis.** Aggressive, early, guided by the PA catheter so that the RV preload is not removed faster than the RV can tolerate. This is the one intervention everyone agrees on. [REVIEW]
3. **Inhaled nitric oxide.** Widely used and physiologically plausible: it dilates vessels in ventilated units and improves V/Q matching, and in a patient whose PVR is drifting up it may reduce RV afterload. Small studies after PTE have shown improved oxygenation and hemodynamics without a mortality signal, and a randomized comparison of inhaled iloprost against iNO after PTE in patients with residual PH found both improved hemodynamics. It is reasonable here for oxygenation, provided it is recognized as symptomatic treatment and weaned deliberately. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]
4. **Steroids.** The habit to question. High-dose methylprednisolone was used for years on the theory that reperfusion injury is inflammatory. The UCSD randomized trial (Kerr and colleagues, Chest 2012) gave perioperative methylprednisolone or placebo and found no reduction in the incidence of lung injury (roughly 41 versus 45 percent) despite measurable reductions in plasma and lavage cytokines. There is no good evidence for steroids once injury is established either. Some centers still give them. The honest position is that they are unproven for prevention and unstudied for treatment. [VERIFY]
5. **Prone positioning.** Reasonable physiology for a localized dependent process and used in some PTE centers for severe injury, but it is a sternotomy patient with chest tubes, a PA catheter, and a vulnerable RV, and the logistical risk is real. It belongs after ventilation, diuresis, and iNO have been tried and before ECMO, in a center that prones cardiac surgical patients routinely. [REVIEW]
6. **ECMO.** VV ECMO for refractory hypoxemia with a functioning RV, VA for hypoxemia with RV failure. Reperfusion injury is a self-limited process over days in most patients, which makes it one of the better indications for ECMO as a bridge to recovery. The decision should be made before the patient has been on an FiO2 of 1.0 and a high PEEP for hours, and the trigger is a trajectory, not a number. [REVIEW] [NMH protocol, insert]

**What not to do:** chase the oxygen saturation with volume because the CVP looks low, start antibiotics for an infiltrate that appeared six hours after an operation on those exact segments, or use the appearance of the radiograph as a reason to delay diuresis.

stages.title: Decision point
stages.narrative:
Postoperative day 1, early morning. Oxygenation has stabilized on iNO, moderate PEEP, and diuresis, and the FiO2 has come down somewhat. Over the past three hours, though, the hemodynamics have changed. PA pressures have climbed and are now approaching the preoperative values. The PVR, calculated from the PA catheter, has risen well above the post-bypass number. Cardiac index has fallen and mixed venous saturation is lower. The CVP is rising. Systemic pressure is maintained on a vasopressor dose that has doubled. Lactate has started to climb. Urine output, which was brisk on the diuretic, has slowed. [REVIEW]

Bedside echo: the RV is more dilated than on arrival, the free wall is hypokinetic, the septum is flattened in systole and diastole, there is now moderate tricuspid regurgitation, and the LV is small and underfilled with vigorous contraction. [REVIEW]

The surgeon, reviewing the numbers, says the left side was always going to be the problem. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Is this residual pulmonary hypertension, worsening reperfusion injury, or both, and how do you tell? Then commit to a vasoactive plan: which pulmonary vasodilator, which inotrope, which vasopressor, and why. State the specific hazard of systemic hypotension in this patient and the criteria that would move you to VA ECMO.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Both, and the distinction matters because the treatments diverge.** Reperfusion injury is a lung parenchymal problem: hypoxemia, infiltrates, high airway pressures, and a PVR that rises modestly through hypoxic vasoconstriction and alveolar compression. Residual pulmonary hypertension is a vascular problem: the PVR did not fall because distal disease was not removed, or it has risen again because of pulmonary vasoconstriction superimposed on a bed that cannot accommodate the cardiac output. Residual PH is the leading cause of death after PTE in the large series, and its risk was predictable from the handoff: the surgeon's dissatisfaction with the left side and more segmental material on the preoperative angiogram. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]

**How to tell:**

- **PVR trajectory relative to the post-bypass baseline.** A PVR that is approaching the preoperative value, in a patient whose oxygenation is stable, is residual PH. Reperfusion injury alone rarely drives the PVR back to where it started. [REVIEW]
- **Oxygenation versus hemodynamics.** The oxygenation has stabilized while the hemodynamics have deteriorated. If reperfusion injury were the driver, they would have moved together.
- **The response to removing the reversible contributors.** Correct hypoxemia, hypercapnia, acidosis, and excessive airway pressure. Check that the iNO is still being delivered. Whatever PVR remains after that is fixed disease plus vasoconstriction, and the vasoconstrictor component is what the pulmonary vasodilators can treat.
- **The wedge pressure and the LV.** A small, underfilled, hyperdynamic LV with a flattened septum says the problem is upstream. This is not LV failure and it is not tamponade, though tamponade must be excluded on every echo in a post-sternotomy patient with a rising CVP.

**The vasoactive plan.**

- **Pulmonary vasodilator.** iNO is already running. Confirm delivery and dose. Inhaled prostacyclin (epoprostenol or iloprost) is the alternative or addition: the randomized comparison after PTE found both reduced PA pressure and PVR. Intravenous pulmonary vasodilators (prostacyclin, sildenafil, milrinone as a vasodilator) carry the cost of systemic hypotension and loss of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, which in a patient with reperfusion injury means worse shunt. Inhaled agents go first. Oral therapy (riociguat, which is the agent licensed for residual or inoperable CTEPH) is for the weeks that follow, not for tonight. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]
- **Inotrope.** Milrinone is the natural first choice because it is an inodilator and lowers PVR, but its systemic vasodilation and long half-life are exactly the wrong properties in a patient whose RV coronary perfusion depends on systemic pressure, and it will increase the vasopressor requirement. Dobutamine has a similar profile with a shorter half-life and more tachycardia. Low-dose epinephrine gives inotropy with pressor support and is a reasonable choice when the systemic pressure is the limiting problem, at the cost of tachycardia, arrhythmia, and lactate. The combination of a low-dose inodilator with a vasopressor is the most common pattern. There is no trial that settles this. [REVIEW]
- **Vasopressor.** Norepinephrine, titrated to a systemic pressure that keeps the RV coronary perfusion gradient positive. Vasopressin is the alternative and has the theoretical advantage of pulmonary vasodilation at low doses with systemic vasoconstriction, which makes it attractive in RV failure, though the evidence is largely from animal and small human studies. Phenylephrine raises PVR and should be avoided. [REVIEW]

**The specific hazard of systemic hypotension.** The RV is perfused throughout the cardiac cycle because its intracavitary pressure is normally low. When the RV is dilated and its systolic pressure is high, as it is here, RV coronary flow becomes diastolic-dependent, and the gradient driving it is the difference between aortic diastolic pressure and RV end-diastolic pressure. A rising CVP and a falling systemic pressure squeeze that gradient from both sides. The result is RV ischemia, further dilation, more tricuspid regurgitation, more septal shift, less LV filling, and less systemic pressure: the spiral. The single most important hemodynamic target in this patient is therefore the systemic pressure, and a vasopressor is RV therapy, not something to be minimized. [REVIEW]

**When VA ECMO.** The honest answer is: earlier than most people do it. Residual PH after PTE does not improve with time in the way reperfusion injury does, so ECMO here is a bridge to a decision (reassessment of the anatomy, balloon pulmonary angioplasty of residual segmental disease, medical therapy, or in rare cases transplantation) rather than a bridge to recovery, and the conversation about what the exit is should happen before cannulation. The criteria that move the decision are a rising lactate despite optimized support, escalating vasopressor and inotrope doses, worsening end-organ function, or an echo that shows the RV losing ground on maximal therapy. Peripheral VA ECMO unloads the RV by draining the RA and supports systemic pressure, and in a patient with an underfilled LV the afterload cost is tolerable. Central cannulation is an option through the fresh sternotomy if the chest must be reopened for another reason. [REVIEW] [NMH protocol, insert]

The conversation with the surgeon and the pulmonary hypertension team about balloon pulmonary angioplasty for the residual left-sided disease should start now, even if it is a procedure for weeks from now, because it changes the exit strategy if ECMO becomes necessary.

stages.title: Complication
stages.narrative: Postoperative day 1, afternoon. Heparin was restarted overnight per the usual schedule, the RV has stabilized on epinephrine, norepinephrine, iNO, and inhaled prostacyclin, and the PVR has come down somewhat. Then the nurse suctions the endotracheal tube and returns a large volume of bright red blood. Over the next few minutes the airway pressures rise sharply, the saturation falls, and the blood keeps coming. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Manage this in the first ten minutes, then the next hour. Cover bronchoscopy, lung isolation, what you do with the heparin, the ECMO question, and what this complication means for the patient's long-term outcome.
questions.modelAnswer:
Airway hemorrhage after PTE is a surgical complication of the endarterectomy plane: the dissection has gone through the arterial wall into the airway, or a distal segmental vessel has disrupted, and reperfusion at full pressure through a fresh plane has found the way out. It is uncommon in the large series, on the order of one to two percent, and it is one of the most dangerous things that happens after this operation. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]

**The first ten minutes.**

- **Oxygenate and protect the other lung.** FiO2 to 1.0, PEEP up (PEEP tamponades bleeding and recruits flooded alveoli), suction to clear what can be cleared, and call for bronchoscopy, a double-lumen tube or bronchial blocker, the surgeon, and the ECMO team at the same time. Do not wait to see whether it stops. [REVIEW]
- **Bronchoscopy, immediately, through the existing tube.** The purpose is localization, not therapy. The surgeon's handoff already told you the left side was the harder dissection, which is the first guess. Find the side, and if possible the lobe, from which the blood is coming. Fresh blood welling from one mainstem with a clear contralateral side is the finding that allows isolation. [REVIEW]
- **Isolation.** Once the side is known, isolate it. Options: advance the single-lumen tube into the contralateral mainstem (fast, crude, adequate for the right side, harder for the left), place a bronchial blocker in the bleeding side under bronchoscopic guidance, or exchange for a double-lumen tube. The double-lumen tube gives the best control and allows the non-bleeding lung to be ventilated while the bleeding side is tamponaded, but the exchange in a hypoxemic, hemodynamically fragile patient with a full airway of blood is itself a dangerous procedure. The bronchial blocker is the usual compromise. Whichever is chosen, the bleeding lung is then deliberately not ventilated, or ventilated with PEEP alone, to let the pressure in the airway tamponade the source. [REVIEW]
- **Stop the heparin.** Immediately. The question of reversal with protamine is harder: the patient has a lifelong thrombotic disorder, fresh endarterectomy surfaces, and an RV that will not survive a new pulmonary embolus, and reversing anticoagulation in that setting is a real risk. If the bleeding is life-threatening and the heparin has been running for hours, reversal is justified, with the surgeon's agreement. If the bleeding is controllable with isolation and PEEP, stopping the infusion and letting it wear off is the more measured course. [REVIEW]
- **Correct the coagulopathy** that the rest of the postoperative course has produced: platelets, fibrinogen, and factors as the labs direct. [REVIEW]

**The next hour.**

- **ECMO as rescue.** If isolation does not restore oxygenation, or if the RV fails under the combined load of hypoxemia and the airway pressures needed to control the bleeding, ECMO is the rescue. The paradox is obvious: ECMO requires anticoagulation and the patient is bleeding. The practical answer, supported by the Mainz group's experience (Guth and colleagues, JTCVS) with VA ECMO after full protamine for massive endobronchial hemorrhage at the end of PTE, is that short-term ECMO can be run with minimal or no systemic anticoagulation, with the circuit accepting a higher clot risk, while the bleeding lung is left unventilated and allowed to tamponade. In their series most patients were weaned within an hour, though that was intraoperative bleeding at separation from bypass rather than a day-1 event. VA rather than VV because the RV is already failing: VA drains the RA, takes the cardiac output out of the pulmonary circulation, drops the PA pressure, and reduces the pressure driving the bleeding. VV ECMO oxygenates but leaves the full cardiac output flowing through the bleeding vessel. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]
- **Definitive control.** Rarely, the bleeding is a discrete vessel that can be embolized, and bronchial or pulmonary angiography with embolization is an option once the patient is stable enough to move. Surgical options (lobectomy, re-exploration) are last resorts. Most airway hemorrhage after PTE is controlled by isolation and time. [REVIEW]
- **When to resume anticoagulation.** Not tonight. The timing is a judgment that balances the patient's thrombotic risk, the ECMO circuit if there is one, and the bleeding, and it is made with the surgeon daily. [NMH protocol, insert]

**What this means for the long term.** This patient has had the three major complications of PTE in 36 hours: reperfusion lung injury, residual pulmonary hypertension, and airway hemorrhage. Each on its own is survivable, and in experienced centers the operative mortality of PTE is now in the low single digits. Together they mark a patient whose distal disease was not fully removable, whose RV has not been relieved of its afterload, and who will leave the ICU with residual CTEPH. The exit strategy is medical therapy (riociguat is licensed for persistent or recurrent CTEPH after PTE), balloon pulmonary angioplasty for accessible residual segmental disease once the lungs have healed, and in a small number of patients transplantation. The ERS statement and the 2022 ESC/ERS guideline both set out this pathway, which is now standard in expert centers and is the reason a PTE program needs a BPA program next to it. The fellow's job in the next week is to keep the RV alive long enough for that pathway to be available. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]

teachingPoints:
- The first night after PTE is predicted by the handoff: the number and duration of circulatory arrest periods, the quality of the specimen on each side, the PVR change off bypass, and whether there was blood in the airway on reperfusion. Ask for these specifically.
- The post-bypass PA pressure, PVR, and cardiac output are the baseline. Every later PA catheter reading is judged against them, not against normal values.
- Avoid hypoxemia and hypercapnia. This is one of the few ICU patients in whom permissive hypercapnia is not an acceptable tradeoff, because PVR and the RV are the problem.
- Reperfusion lung injury is a localized, high-permeability edema in the endarterectomized segments, appearing in the first 24 to 72 hours, with a low wedge pressure. Diuresis and lung-protective ventilation are the treatment. Steroids did not prevent it in the one randomized trial. [VERIFY]
- Pulmonary vasodilators are not routine after PTE. They are symptomatic therapy for residual PH with hemodynamic compromise, and inhaled agents are preferred because systemic agents cost systemic pressure and hypoxic vasoconstriction. [VERIFY]
- Residual PH and reperfusion injury are distinguished by the PVR trajectory relative to the post-bypass baseline and by whether oxygenation and hemodynamics move together. They often coexist.
- The RV's coronary perfusion depends on the gradient between aortic diastolic pressure and RV end-diastolic pressure. A vasopressor that protects systemic pressure is RV therapy. Phenylephrine raises PVR and is the wrong vasopressor.
- VA ECMO for residual PH is a bridge to a decision, not to recovery. The exit (BPA, medical therapy, transplant) should be named before cannulation.
- Airway hemorrhage after PTE is managed by localization with bronchoscopy, isolation of the bleeding lung, PEEP as tamponade, stopping heparin, and VA ECMO with minimal anticoagulation as rescue. Reversal of heparin is a judgment, not a reflex, in a patient with a lifelong thrombotic disorder.
pitfalls:
- Starting iNO for early hypoxemia without deciding whether the problem is the lung or the vasculature.
- Treating a low CVP as a volume deficit in a patient with leaky endarterectomized lungs and an RV that is already full.
- Allowing hypercapnia in the name of lung protection in a patient whose RV cannot afford the PVR.
- Starting antibiotics for an infiltrate that appeared within hours of the operation in the operated segments.
- Choosing milrinone for RV support without a plan for the systemic hypotension it causes.
- Using phenylephrine to treat hypotension in a patient with RV failure.
- Waiting for lactate and end-organ failure to declare the need for ECMO in residual PH, where time does not heal.
- Reversing heparin reflexively for airway bleeding without weighing the thrombotic risk of a patient with CTEPH and fresh endarterectomy surfaces, or conversely continuing heparin while the airway fills with blood.
- Choosing VV rather than VA ECMO for airway hemorrhage when the RV is failing and the PA pressure is driving the bleeding.
controversies:
**Steroids for reperfusion lung injury.** High-dose methylprednisolone was standard in many PTE programs for decades on an inflammatory rationale. The UCSD randomized placebo-controlled trial (Kerr 2012) found no reduction in the incidence of lung injury despite measurable cytokine suppression. Some centers continue to use perioperative steroids, citing the trial's size and the heterogeneity of injury definitions. There is no evidence for or against steroids as treatment of established injury. The defensible position is that they are unproven. [VERIFY]

**Routine inhaled nitric oxide.** Some programs start iNO on every patient in the OR and wean it over the first days, on the grounds that it is safe, improves oxygenation, and reduces RV afterload during the most vulnerable period. Others, including the UCSD program as published, use it selectively for residual PH with hemodynamic compromise, arguing that it is a device with a weaning problem, that rebound on withdrawal is real, and that in the absence of residual PH the benefit is cosmetic. Small studies show improved oxygenation and hemodynamics. None shows a mortality difference. [VERIFY] [NMH protocol, insert]

**ECMO timing and configuration.** For reperfusion injury, ECMO as a bridge to recovery has good outcomes in experienced centers because the injury is self-limited. For residual PH, outcomes are worse because there is nothing to recover to without a further intervention. Where the line sits between early ECMO as a strategy and ECMO as salvage is unsettled, and so is the choice between VV (for isolated hypoxemia) and VA (for RV failure, or for bleeding where dropping the PA pressure matters). Centers vary widely in how early they cannulate and whether they use peripheral or central access in the fresh sternotomy. [REVIEW] [NMH protocol, insert]

**Balloon pulmonary angioplasty for residual disease.** BPA has moved from a salvage procedure to a standard part of the CTEPH pathway in expert centers, endorsed by the ERS statement and the 2022 ESC/ERS guideline for inoperable and residual disease. What is not settled is timing after PTE (how long to wait for the endarterectomized surfaces to heal and for the reperfusion injury to resolve), whether BPA should be offered to patients with modestly elevated residual PVR who are asymptomatic, and whether a planned hybrid strategy (PTE for proximal disease, early BPA for distal disease) should be the default for patients like this one. Medical therapy with riociguat is the licensed alternative, and the sequencing of drug versus BPA versus both is center-dependent. [VERIFY]

**Fluid strategy.** Everyone agrees on restriction and early diuresis. No one agrees on how far to push it in a patient whose RV is preload-dependent, and the PA catheter is the only arbiter. The use of colloid, the transfusion threshold, and the diuretic strategy are institutional. [NMH protocol, insert]
discussWithAttending: The resident wants to start iNO at ninety minutes for a falling saturation. Argue for it, then argue against it, and say what single piece of data would decide you.

The PVR has climbed back toward preoperative values on day 1 and the lactate is rising on epinephrine and norepinephrine. How early is too early for VA ECMO in residual PH, and what exit would you need to have named before cannulating?
Heparin has been running for six hours and the airway is full of blood. Protamine or not? Make the case both ways for a patient with CTEPH and fresh endarterectomy surfaces.
Milrinone, dobutamine, or epinephrine for this RV, and which vasopressor alongside it? Defend your choice against the physiological objection to each.
This patient will leave the ICU with residual CTEPH. Who should own the decision between riociguat, balloon pulmonary angioplasty, and both, and when after PTE should BPA be considered?
